--- title: "Combining viewing directions around Martigny" guide-section: "Tutorials" bread-crumbs: false execute: freeze: true --- # Combining viewing directions around Martigny This tutorial runs the whole pipeline, from search to composites, for a small area around Martigny in the Swiss canton of Valais. The town lies on the flat floor of the Rhône valley, where the river bends to the north, between steep slopes that face in many directions. It compares a composite of the ascending orbits, one of the descending orbits, and one that combines both with local resolution weighting (LRW). ## Find the grid squares and their bursts The area is a box of about 7 by 9 km around the town. It touches four 10 km squares of the MGRS grid, all in UTM zone 32 North. The composites cover these squares whole, so the search covers them too, through the union of their bounding boxes, as in [From an area to composites](area-to-composites.qmd#set-up). It returns every VV burst of August 2025 that overlaps them: ::: {#b4be5231 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import shapely from shapely.geometry import box from s1bursts import ( BurstCatalog, BurstProcessor, FileManager, MGRSGrid, ResolutionWeighter, RTCConfig, SearchQuery, TimeRange, ) fm = FileManager("data/martigny") catalog = BurstCatalog(fm) aoi = box(7.03, 46.06, 7.12, 46.14) window = TimeRange("2025-08-01", "2025-08-31") squares = list(MGRSGrid(aoi, resolution=20)) print(", ".join(square.mgrs_code for square in squares), {str(square.crs) for square in squares}) search_area = shapely.union_all([box(*square.geographic_extent.boundingbox) for square in squares]) bursts = catalog.search(SearchQuery(time_range=window, intersects=search_area, polarization="VV")) bursts.df.groupby(["pass_direction", "rel_orbit_number"]).agg( acquisitions=("date", lambda dates: dates.dt.date.nunique()), bursts=("burst_id", "size"), sub_swaths=("sub_swath", lambda names: ", ".join(sorted(names.unique()))), satellites=("parent_product_name", lambda names: ", ".join(sorted(names.str[:3].unique()))), ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 32TLS40, 32TLS41, 32TLS50, 32TLS51 {'EPSG:32632'} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}
acquisitions bursts sub_swaths satellites
pass_direction rel_orbit_number
Ascending 88 5 10 IW2 S1A, S1C
Descending 66 5 15 IW3 S1A, S1C
139 5 25 IW1, IW2 S1A, S1C
``` ::: ::: Three relative orbits cover the squares: orbit 88 on ascending passes, in the evening, and orbits 66 and 139 on descending passes, in the morning. Each orbit was imaged five times in August, by Sentinel-1A and Sentinel-1C in turn. Orbit 88 needs two bursts per acquisition to cover the squares, orbit 66 three, and orbit 139 five, from two neighbouring sub-swaths, which makes 50 bursts in total. The descending orbits contribute twice as many acquisitions as the ascending one. ## Process the bursts Since the squares share one zone, all 50 bursts are processed in one batch, in that zone, at the 20 m pixel size of the composites. This follows the [AOI-first order](area-to-composites.qmd#aoi-first): ::: {#0954ddc1 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} catalog.download(bursts).raise_on_failure() processor = BurstProcessor(fm) rtc = processor.create_backscatter( bursts, crs=squares[0].crs, config=RTCConfig(grid_spacing=20), ).raise_on_failure().products ``` ::: ## Compose every square Each square is composed from the products whose bursts reach it, twice: once per pass direction with `compose_rtc_by_pass()`, and once across both directions with `compose_rtc_lrw()`, which also writes the quality layers. ::: {#672e13f5 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} weighter = ResolutionWeighter(fm) lrw, by_pass = [], [] for square in squares: footprints = {(b.burst_id, b.sub_swath) for b in bursts.intersecting(square)} square_rtc = [p for p in rtc if (p.burst_id, p.sub_swath) in footprints] lrw.append(weighter.compose_rtc_lrw(square_rtc, square, write_qa=True, time_range=window)) by_pass.append(weighter.compose_rtc_by_pass(square_rtc, square, time_range=window)) print(f"{square.mgrs_code}: {len(square_rtc)} bursts") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 32TLS40: 35 bursts 32TLS41: 40 bursts 32TLS50: 25 bursts 32TLS51: 30 bursts ``` ::: ::: ## Compare the viewing directions Sentinel-1 looks to the right of its track. On ascending passes it flies roughly north and looks east, so slopes facing west are turned towards it; on descending passes it flies south and looks west, towards slopes facing east. A slope turned towards the radar is squeezed into few pixels and seen coarsely, and one turned away is stretched over many pixels and seen finely, unless it is so steep that the radar cannot see it at all. Such a slope lies in radar shadow, and the products of that direction have no value there. The figure joins the four squares of each composite into one mosaic and shows the area of interest. Red marks the pixels without a value, which a pass composite has where its direction sees only radar shadow. The rectangles mark three sample areas: the valley floor east of the town (white), a slope facing north-west (yellow) and one facing north-east (cyan). ::: {#5e468864 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import numpy as np import pandas as pd from rasterio.merge import merge from rasterio.transform import rowcol from rasterio.warp import transform_bounds from s1bursts.product import Layer def mosaic(composites, layer=Layer.MEASUREMENT): """Join the squares of one layer; return the data and its transform.""" data, transform = merge([fm.get_product_path(c, layer) for c in composites]) return data[0].astype("float32"), transform def km_extent(data, transform): """Return the extent of a mosaic in kilometres, for imshow.""" rows, cols = data.shape left, top = transform.c, transform.f return [v / 1000 for v in (left, left + transform.a * cols, top + transform.e * rows, top)] crs = squares[0].crs composites = { "Ascending": mosaic([c["Ascending"] for c in by_pass]), "Descending": mosaic([c["Descending"] for c in by_pass]), "LRW": mosaic(lrw), } areas = { "valley floor": (box(7.100, 46.110, 7.115, 46.120), "white"), "slope facing north-west": (box(7.031, 46.115, 7.038, 46.119), "gold"), "slope facing north-east": (box(7.043, 46.110, 7.050, 46.114), "tab:cyan"), } view = transform_bounds("EPSG:4326", crs, *aoi.bounds) gray = plt.get_cmap("gray").copy() gray.set_bad("tab:red") # pixels without a value: radar shadow fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 5.2), sharey=True, layout="constrained") for ax, (name, (data, transform)) in zip(axes, composites.items()): image = ax.imshow(10 * np.log10(data), extent=km_extent(data, transform), cmap=gray, vmin=-20, vmax=0) for area, colour in areas.values(): x0, y0, x1, y1 = transform_bounds("EPSG:4326", crs, *area.bounds) ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((x0 / 1000, y0 / 1000), (x1 - x0) / 1000, (y1 - y0) / 1000, fill=False, edgecolor=colour, linewidth=1.5)) ax.set(title=name, xlabel="Easting (km)", xlim=(view[0] / 1000, view[2] / 1000), ylim=(view[1] / 1000, view[3] / 1000)) axes[0].set_ylabel("Northing (km)") fig.colorbar(image, ax=axes, shrink=0.8, label="Gamma-0 (dB)") plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Backscatter composites of August 2025 around Martigny: the five ascending acquisitions (left), the ten descending acquisitions (middle), and all fifteen combined with local resolution weighting (right). Red marks radar shadow, where a composite has no value.](martigny-composite_files/figure-html/cell-6-output-1.png){width=1160 height=467} ::: ::: The median of each composite in the three sample areas puts numbers on the comparison. The medians are taken in linear units and converted to decibels afterwards, and they skip the pixels without a value: ::: {#1a4e6d03 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} def median_in(data, transform, area): """Median of a mosaic within a lon/lat rectangle.""" x0, y0, x1, y1 = transform_bounds("EPSG:4326", crs, *area.bounds) (top, bottom), (left, right) = rowcol(transform, [x0, x1], [y1, y0]) return np.nanmedian(data[top:bottom, left:right]) pd.DataFrame({ name: { area_name: 10 * np.log10(median_in(data, transform, area)) for area_name, (area, _) in areas.items() } for name, (data, transform) in composites.items() }).round(1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ```{=html}
Ascending Descending LRW
valley floor -9.8 -10.6 -10.2
slope facing north-west -7.2 -9.7 -9.3
slope facing north-east -8.4 -6.9 -7.7
``` ::: ::: How much of each area a composite misses in shadow: ::: {#5e208874 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} def share_missing(data, transform, area): """Share of a mosaic's pixels without a value within a lon/lat rectangle.""" x0, y0, x1, y1 = transform_bounds("EPSG:4326", crs, *area.bounds) (top, bottom), (left, right) = rowcol(transform, [x0, x1], [y1, y0]) return np.isnan(data[top:bottom, left:right]).mean() pd.DataFrame({ name: { area_name: f"{share_missing(data, transform, area):.1%}" for area_name, (area, _) in areas.items() } for name, (data, transform) in composites.items() }) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ```{=html}
Ascending Descending LRW
valley floor 0.0% 0.0% 0.0%
slope facing north-west 0.0% 22.4% 0.0%
slope facing north-east 13.5% 0.0% 0.0%
``` ::: ::: On the valley floor the three composites look alike: the fields, the town and the river show the same pattern in each. The ascending composite is 0.8 dB brighter there than the descending one, an offset that is close to uniform across the floor and comes from the different times of day and incidence angles of the two directions rather than from the terrain. The LRW composite lies between the two. On the slopes, the difference between the directions changes with the way the slope faces. Each direction smears the slopes turned towards it into coarse streaks and reads them brighter, and it loses the steepest slopes turned away from it to shadow. The slope facing north-west is 2.5 dB brighter in the ascending composite than in the descending one, which has no value on 22.4 % of it. The slope facing north-east is 1.5 dB brighter in the descending composite, and the ascending one has no value on 13.5 % of it. The LRW composite has a value everywhere: where one direction sees only shadow, it takes the pixel from the other. Elsewhere it leans towards the direction that sees each slope from behind. On the north-west slope it is within 0.4 dB of the descending composite. On the north-east slope it lies about midway, although the descending orbits supply two thirds of the acquisitions; their squeezed view of that slope gets less weight. Across the map, the LRW composite keeps the sharper view of each slope. ## Read the quality layers The LRW composite comes with two quality layers. The figure shows them for the four squares, with the composite for reference: ::: {#8178021d .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} from matplotlib.colors import LogNorm layers = { "LRW composite (dB)": (Layer.MEASUREMENT, dict(cmap="gray", vmin=-20, vmax=0)), "QA-NUM": (Layer.QA_NUM, dict(cmap="viridis", vmin=0, vmax=15)), "QA-CQM": (Layer.QA_CQM, dict(cmap="magma", norm=LogNorm(0.25, 4))), } fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 4.6), sharey=True, layout="constrained") for ax, (title, (layer, style)) in zip(axes, layers.items()): data, transform = mosaic(lrw, layer) if layer == Layer.MEASUREMENT: data = 10 * np.log10(data) fig.colorbar(ax.imshow(data, extent=km_extent(data, transform), **style), ax=ax, shrink=0.8) ax.set(title=title, xlabel="Easting (km)") axes[0].set_ylabel("Northing (km)") plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![The LRW composite of the four grid squares (left), the number of acquisitions that contributed to each pixel, QA-NUM (middle), and the composite quality, QA-CQM, on a logarithmic scale (right).](martigny-composite_files/figure-html/cell-9-output-1.png){width=1162 height=381} ::: ::: ::: {#1149ba90 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} num, _ = mosaic(lrw, Layer.QA_NUM) cqm, transform = mosaic(lrw, Layer.QA_CQM) floor, _ = areas["valley floor"] shares = pd.Series(num.ravel()).value_counts(normalize=True) print("Share of pixels by QA-NUM:", {n: f"{shares.get(n, 0):.1%}" for n in (15, 10, 5)}) print(f"QA-CQM on the valley floor: {median_in(cqm, transform, floor):.2f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Share of pixels by QA-NUM: {15: '94.1%', 10: '3.4%', 5: '0.7%'} QA-CQM on the valley floor: 0.83 ``` ::: ::: `QA-NUM` counts the acquisitions that carry weight in each pixel. All fifteen contribute almost everywhere, on 94 % of the four squares and on the whole valley floor. The exceptions are the steepest slopes, where one direction looks into radar shadow and its acquisitions get no weight. Ten acquisitions remain where one orbit drops out, on 3.4 % of the squares: the ascending one on slopes facing east, or one of the descending ones on slopes facing west. On a few very steep slopes facing west, 0.7 % of the squares, both descending orbits see shadow and only the five ascending acquisitions remain. `QA-CQM` rates the combined resolution of each pixel. It is nearly constant on the valley floor, about 0.83, since flat ground is seen alike from every orbit. It is highest on the slopes facing west, which the ten descending acquisitions see from behind and in fine detail, and lowest on the steepest slopes, which every acquisition sees squeezed or not at all. A pixel with a low `QA-CQM` is reported at the same 20 m as the others but describes the ground more coarsely; [Local resolution weighting](resolution-weighting.qmd) explains both layers. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Run details Run on 02 November 2026 with s1bursts 0.7.1.dev35+g189a2f464.d20261102 and ESA SNAP 13.0.0. Contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data (2025). :::
